newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - TV execs face increasingly frenetic competition.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - TV execs face increasingly frenetic competition.

text.p: The explosive growth of cable, satellite and digital television in Europe has shaken up the industry and is making life increasingly frenetic for TV executives, experts say.
Delegates who attended the six-day MIP television trade show in Cannes this month presented a microcosm of the kind of razor-sharp competition now facing international entertainment executives.

Many of the 2,700 delegates from 103 countries who attended the fair in the French Riviera resort of Cannes said they spent most of their time rushing around frantically making contacts and doing deals.

Television broadcasters from Europe, the United States and Asia were scrambling to buy programmes that would help them attract advertisers and prevent fickle viewers hopping away to a growing number of new channels.
Entertainment production houses use the yearly MIP fair, which ended on April 16, to sell their wares.
EUROPE-U.S PARTNERSHIPS

Variety, the U.S. entertainment publication, said the MIP trade show created some strange bedfellows, including European public broadcasters who are now teaming up with commercial TV companies in the United States.

Big American television studios are also coddling small documentary film makers and companies that are arch rivals in some areas of business are buying and selling to each other as though they were the best of friends, Variety said.
Late last year the heavyweights of French digital television, Canalsatellite and Television Par Satellite (TPS) cut major deals with big American players.

Canalsatellite, which is owned by French pay television company Canal Plus, was launched in April 1996. TPS, which is operated by French private terrestrial channel Tlvision Franaise 1 and ABSat, is part of AB Productions.
Delegates at Cannes said the trade show was a mad, unending crunch of business contacts.
"We don't have time to see the sun. MIP is 200 meetings in six days," Daniel Ziv, founder of French production house Dix Francs, told Reuters.
"I can't even read my diary, I've got a meeting every 15 minutes," said a breathless Guillermo Spivak, chairman of Franco-Argentinian company In Deed.
John Kuyk, purchasing and derivative products director at Canada's Canal Vie, part of Radiomutuel Inc, reckoned he had done alright in Cannes.
"I bought 700 hours of programmes for 1.4 million dollars," he told Reuters, adding that he was heading for Paris to do more deals and build "alliances" with thematic TV channels.
HOLDING ON TO AUDIENCES/ADVERTISERS
MIP provided a glimpse of how big television channels are trying to hold onto prime-time audiences and advertisers.

The French channel, TF1, announced at Cannes that the film star Gerard Depardieu would star in and co-produce a mini-series television remake of Alexander Dumas's famous novel, "The Count of Monte Cristo".
With a provisional budget of 90 million francs ($15.5 million), it will be the most expensive television fiction production in France.
French digital television companies, although their services are still new, seized the occasion to vaunt subscriber numbers and growth projections.

Canalsatellite said it had 500,000 subscribers, including 300,000 for its digital service, while TPS said it had 116,000 subscribers and forecast 300,000 by the end of the year -- more than originally projected.
Despite the scramble in Cannes, the price of television programmes has not risen dramatically, delegates said.
"Overall it (price) is stable, as far as one can see," said Jean-Jacques Silberstein, programmes director at France's third digital satellite service ABSat.
